POD-596 · Design audit · Usage & analytics

They put a message next to every number. We put a fact.

Two usage dashboards, audited against the same rubric. Ours wins on honesty and information density. Theirs wins on something we barely attempt: making each figure mean something without the reader doing arithmetic. That gap is closeable with data we already compute.

Method — /impeccable critique, degraded: single-context (this project's agent policy blocks the two-subagent split the playbook requires; both assessments were run in one context).
Ours — captured live off worktree-POD-596, real operator data, 1600×1100 @2x. Theirs — operator-supplied screenshot; static, so interaction heuristics are read as unknown, not scored.
Detector — detect.mjs over features/usage/: 0 findings. Everything below is judgment, not lint.

The evidence

Same job, two philosophies.

What ours does better

  • 168 columns, not 30 smoothed points. The hour trace shows the overnight runs, the dead Sunday, the hour a fleet went wide. Their chart shows seven shapes and interpolates between them.
  • Tokens against cost, side by side. Cache read is 97.4% of the tokens and 69.0% of the bill; output is 0.3% of tokens and 12.7% of cost. Neither their page nor any tool I know draws that comparison. It is the one genuinely non-obvious reading on either screen.
  • No cards, and no false precision. Hairline division instead of a metric grid; $11,882 instead of $371,945.49 on a modelled estimate.
  • Honest empty hours. An hour that ran nothing draws nothing. Their area chart has no way to say "nothing happened here" — it just slopes.
  • The loading state is the real layout. Unfilled slots in the finished geometry, not a skeleton with its own second geometry to maintain.

What theirs does better

  • Every figure carries a second figure that interprets it. 571B processed → "21.2B per active day". 558B cached → "97.8% of observed input". 967M output → "includes 328M reasoning". Not labels. Comparisons.
  • Cache savings is a headline, not a share. "$2,512,686.42 · 6.8× the raw token cost" turns a statistic into news. We hold the same number and report it as "69.0%".
  • The caveat is attached to the number. $371,945.49* with "* if billed at full API rate" directly beneath. Ours states the same caveat 700px away in the footer.
  • The window is dated. "Jul 10 to Aug 8" under the title. Ours says "Last 7 days" and never names them.
  • Who spent it, before which model spent it. Two provider rows with a share meter answer "Codex or Claude?" in one glance. Our four-row model table makes you add it up.

The transferable idea

Five moves worth taking, one worth inventing. None needs new data.

Each row states their move, then the version that belongs in our sheet — and names the field it comes out of. Everything listed already exists in usageSummary()'s return value or is one division away from it.

01
Their move

A derived comparison under every number

Their stat strip never prints a bare quantity. 571B tokens is followed by "21.2B per active day" — a second number whose only job is to give the first one a scale.

Our version

Sub-lines on the readout, not a stat strip

Keep the one big figure. Give it the rate underneath: $1,980 per active day · 6 of 7 days ran. Move "last 5 hours" into that same line as a rate rather than a second headline.

Data: summary.days[].totalTokens for the active-day count; summary.week and summary.fiveHour already exist. Cost: ~8 lines in UsageReadouts.
02
Their move

Cache savings framed as money not spent

The best sentence on their page. "Cache savings $2,512,686.42 — 6.8× the raw token cost." A cache-hit rate is a statistic; a cache saving is a result.

Our version

One flat line under the readout

Stated as an instrument would, not as marketing: Cache reads bill at 10% of input — $73,782 less than the same tokens uncached, 6.2× the week's whole bill. No badge, no green, no exclamation.

Data: composition.cacheRead.estCostUsd × 9 — the pricing table already discounts cache reads to 0.1×, so the counterfactual is arithmetic on a number we return. Cost: one derived value, one line of markup.
03
Their move

The asterisk lives on the number

You cannot read $371,945.49* without reading "if billed at full API rate". The qualification is unskippable because it is adjacent.

Our version

Promote the cost basis out of the footer

Ten words under the readout: * at API list price — not what you were billed. The footer cell shrinks to the source and the model list; it stops carrying the one caveat that has to travel with the figure.

Data: none. Pure copy move inside UsageProvenance → UsageReadouts.
04
Their move

Name the dates, and rank the providers

"Jul 10 to Aug 8" in the header. Then Codex and Claude Code as two ranked rows with a meter and a dense sub-line each — "98.6% of cost · 566B tokens".

Our version

Date in the sheet header; a two-row provider rollup

The dates go where the sheet's own title bar already has empty space: AUG 02 – AUG 08 · ROLLING. The rollup is the model table grouped by a field every row already carries, drawn with the composition rail we already have.

Data: summary.models[].provider — already derived by bucketProvider(). Group and sum. Cost: a ~20-line component reusing CompCell. Note: their 7/30/90 range switcher is not free — the daemon scans a 7-day window, so a 30-day range means a protocol change and a slower scan. Skipped on purpose.
05
Their move

One chart, two measures

A COST / TOKENS toggle above the plot, and a MODEL / DAY toggle above the table. The same pixels answer two questions instead of committing to one.

Our version

Default the trace to cost

Today the sheet leads with $11,882 and then charts tokens — the headline and the picture measure different things. Flip the default to cost and keep tokens behind a toggle. Every hour slot already carries both.

Data: UsageHour.estCostUsd and .totalTokens — both populated today; only the axis and the peak readout switch formatters. Cost: one piece of local state.
06
Their move

—

Nothing on their page does this. It falls out of the one thing ours already has and theirs doesn't.

Ours to invent

Say the composition comparison out loud

We draw two rails and leave the reader to divide them. One column does the division: cost share ÷ token share. Output reads 42× its weight, cache write 10×, cache read 0.7×. That is the sentence the section exists to say, and it is currently unsaid.

Data: already on screen — estCostUsd/totalCost ÷ tokens/totalTokens. Cost: a fourth grid column.

The proposal

The same sheet, with the messages put back in.

Nothing is removed except the second 24px readout and one footer cell. The trace, the composition rails, the model table and the footer bar are the ones that shipped. Figures are carried from the live capture above.

  • 1One readout, not two. Our own DESIGN.md says the 24px step is "rationed to one figure per surface" — and the sheet currently spends it twice, on $343 and $11,882. The 5-hour figure is a rate, so it reads correctly as a clause in the sub-line and stops competing with the week.
  • 2The cache line. The single highest-value sentence available to this sheet, and it costs one multiplication.
  • 3The caveat moves to the number. The footer's "Cost basis" cell becomes "Pricing", and carries what the footer is actually for: how the figure was produced, not what it means.
  • 4Dates in the header; providers above the fold. Both answer a question the sheet currently forces you to hold in your head.
  • 5The chart measures what the headline measures. Cost by default, tokens one click away.
  • 6The comparison, stated. Two rails plus a ratio column turns a picture into a finding: output is 42× its token weight, so the lever on this bill is response length, not context size.

Mockup figures: the seven readouts, both windows, the composition shares and every model row are carried verbatim from the live capture. The per-day and per-hour cost figures are derived from those at the window's blended rate — the shipped sheet would compute them exactly from UsageDay.estCostUsd and UsageHour.estCostUsd, which are already populated and currently unused by the UI.

Explicitly not copied

Six things their page does that ours should keep refusing.

The smoothed area chartTheir curve is a spline through ~30 daily points. It bulges between samples and invents values that never occurred — a $100k day is drawn as a mountain with slopes on either side. Our columns are the honest form.
The five-cell stat stripThe idea (an interpretive sub-line per figure) is the best thing on their page. The packaging is a bordered metric-card grid — the first named anti-reference in PRODUCT.md. Take the idea, drop the boxes.
Cent-level precision on an estimate$371,945.49 implies an invoice. It is a model of one. Ours already rounds above $100 and should keep doing so.
"Raw token cost" as a labelIt is not raw — it is list-price-modelled. "API-equivalent" is the more accurate phrase and we already use it.
The Cost quality columnFour rows in a full-height column, three of which read 0.0%. The honest, dense version for us is one footer sentence about whether any model fell back to default pricing — which is exactly what PRICING.find(…) ?? DEFAULT_PRICING already knows.
The 7 / 30 / 90 range switcherAttractive, and not free: the daemon scans a rolling 7-day window. A 90-day range is a protocol parameter, a much slower filesystem scan, and a memo that no longer fits. Out of scope by your own constraint, and correctly so.

Scorecard — ours

Nielsen's ten, on the surface I could actually operate.

#HeuristicScoreReading
1Visibility of system status4The staleness stamp, the 400ms-gated refresh hairline and the unfilled-slot cold state are better than most shipping products manage.
2Match to the real world2The weak one. "Last 7 days" is undated; the sheet leads in dollars and charts tokens; cache economics are shown as percentages a person has to convert into meaning.
3User control and freedom3Esc, backdrop and ✕ all close. No control over what is measured — no range, no measure toggle.
4Consistency and standards3On-system throughout, but the surface breaks its own DESIGN.md readout rule by spending the 24px step twice.
5Error prevention4Read-only surface; the <synthetic> row is filtered at both the daemon and the client.
6Recognition over recall2Provider totals, the busiest day in money, and the cache saving all require mental arithmetic over what is on screen.
7Flexibility and efficiency2One view, one window, one measure. No toggles, no grouping, no export.
8Aesthetic and minimalist design4Genuinely excellent. Nothing decorative, nothing boxed, density earned.
9Error recovery4Cold-and-unreachable gets its own state with a retry; a stale reading is labelled rather than silently served.
10Help and documentation3The footer bar is real documentation in the right register — but the caveat it carries is too far from the figure it qualifies.
Total31/40 — strong. The three 2s are all the same failure wearing different clothes: the sheet reports, and does not interpret.

Priority issues

  1. P0

    Every number is a fact; almost none is a message.

    $11,882 · 6.8B tokens · 38,050 replies. Is that a lot? Compared to what? Their sheet answers "compared to what" on every line; ours answers it nowhere. This is the whole gap between the two designs, and it is not a data problem — it is a decision not to divide two numbers we already have.

    Sub-lines 01, 02 and 06 above. Rate per active day on the readout; the cache saving as a stated line; the cost-per-token ratio column on the composition.

  2. P1

    The headline and the chart measure different things.

    The sheet's own comment says it "leads with cost" because tokens are the raw material. Then the largest object on the surface is titled "Tokens per hour". A reader who takes the headline seriously cannot read the picture in the same unit.

    Default the trace to cost with a COST/TOKENS toggle. Both values are on every hour slot today.

  3. P1

    The window is never named.

    "Last 7 days" and "Rolling, counted back from now" are correct and unhelpful when you are trying to reconcile a spike against something you remember doing on Tuesday.

    Date range in the sheet header, where there is already empty space beside the title.

  4. P2

    The 24px readout step is spent twice.

    DESIGN.md — written by this very issue — rations that step to one figure per surface, "because the moment a second number takes it they become a metric-card grid". The sheet has two. The rule is right; the implementation drifted from it.

    Demote the 5-hour figure into the readout's sub-line as a rate.

  5. P2

    No provider rollup, despite carrying provider on every row.

    "Am I spending this on Claude or on Codex?" is the second question anyone asks, and the sheet makes you sum four table rows to answer it.

    Two rows above the trace, reusing the composition rail.

  6. P3

    The cost-basis caveat is 700px from the number it qualifies.

    A reader who never scrolls to the footer bar reads $11,882 as a bill.

    Ten words under the readout; the footer keeps provenance, not meaning.

If you want it built

Every change above lands in three files — UsageView.tsx, usage.ts and the .usage-* block of styles.css. No protocol change, no daemon change, no new query. The heaviest single item is the cost/tokens toggle, because the axis, the peak readout and the day labels all have to switch formatter together.

The cheapest three — the cache-savings line, the ratio column, and the dated header — are together maybe forty lines and carry most of the value. They are what turns the sheet from a correct report into one that tells you something.
